lessons.title: Why farms keep records and what to record
lessons.html:
Records as a management tool

A farm generates data every day: rainfall, animals born and sold, litres of milk, hectares planted, kilograms harvested, litres of diesel, hours worked, rand spent. Data management is the discipline of collecting this data accurately, storing it safely and turning it into information that supports decisions. Without records a farmer relies on memory and guesswork; with records, the farmer can compare blocks, camps and seasons, spot problems early, satisfy buyers and lenders, and meet legal obligations.

Reasons for keeping records

  • Management decisions – which enterprise or cultivar performs best, when to replace a bull, how much fertiliser each block needs.
  • Financial control – tracking income and costs, preparing budgets and tax returns.
  • Legal and market requirements – employee records, chemical application records, animal identification and movement, food safety and traceability for retailers and exporters.
  • Credit – banks and the Land Bank expect evidence of past production and finances.

Types of farm records

CategoryExamples
Physical: cropsPlanting dates, cultivar, area, inputs applied, spray records, yields per block
Physical: livestockAnimal ID, births, deaths, weights, treatments, dipping, sales, stock counts per camp
ResourcesRainfall, irrigation volumes, soil analyses, veld condition
LabourAttendance, hours, tasks, leave, training
AssetsMachinery hours, services, fuel use, buildings and fences
FinancialInvoices, receipts, cash book, bank statements

Primary and secondary records

A primary record is captured at the source, for example a rain gauge reading or a dipping register filled in at the dip tank. A secondary record summarises primary records, for example a monthly rainfall summary or a herd inventory. Errors at the primary stage flow through to every report, so the quality of primary capture is critical.

lessons.title: Designing, capturing and storing records
lessons.html:
Designing a good record

A record form, whether paper or on a tablet, should be simple enough to complete in the field and complete enough to be useful. Good design principles:

  • Capture only what will be used. Ask: what decision will this data support?
  • Use a consistent layout with clear headings and units (kg, ha, mm, litres, R).
  • Include date, location (block, camp, kraal), the person recording and a unique reference such as an animal tag or lot number.
  • Use codes or tick boxes where possible to reduce writing and spelling errors.
  • Keep a column for remarks so unusual events are noted.

Capturing data accurately

  1. Train the people who record. Show them examples of correct entries.
  2. Record at the time of the event, not at the end of the week.
  3. Use calibrated instruments: a checked scale, a level rain gauge, a working flow meter.
  4. Check entries regularly for missing values, impossible values (a 2,000 kg calf) and duplicates.
  5. Correct errors visibly and note who corrected them.

From paper to computer

Many farms capture on paper and enter data later into a spreadsheet or farm management software. Others capture directly on phones or tablets. Spreadsheets are useful for small datasets: one row per event, one column per field, no merged cells, consistent date formats. Dedicated software adds validation, reports and links between records, such as linking a spray record to the stock of chemicals in the store.

Storing and protecting records

  • Keep paper records in a dry, secure place, filed by type and date.
  • Back up electronic data regularly, with a copy stored off the farm or in the cloud.
  • Control access with passwords; not everyone needs to change data.
  • Personal information about employees must be handled lawfully under the Protection of Personal Information Act 4 of 2013.
  • Keep records for the period required by law, by tax rules and by buyers' audit standards.

Key points

  • Records support decisions, financial control, legal compliance and credit.
  • Farm records cover crops, livestock, resources, labour, assets and finances.
  • Primary records captured at the source determine the quality of all reports.
  • Design simple forms with dates, locations, units and unique references.
  • Store records securely, back them up and protect personal information.
